title: If not now, when?
hookLine: Hillel: if I am not for myself, who is for me? if I am only for myself, what am I? if not now, when? (Pirkei Avot 1:14)
tomorrow: strict Shammai had one rule about your face. what was it?

cards: A to-do app usually has a button for later: snooze, someday, remind me tomorrow. Hillel, a sage from the time before the Temple fell, asked the question that button avoids. If I am not for myself, who will be for me?
And if I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? Three questions, in Pirkei Avot.
The last one sounds like a poster. But the Talmud tells of a very long argument, between Hillel's students and the students of his rival, Shammai, that lands in the same place.

teach.b: The Talmud says the house of Shammai and the house of Hillel argued for two and a half years over one question: would it have been better for human beings never to have been created? Let both sides speak.
The Talmud gives only their answers; the reasons here are how teachers put each side's case.

teach.h: SHAMMAI: THE WEIGHT OF A LIFE.
teach.b: The house of Shammai: better not. A human life carries enormous responsibility, and every day brings the chance to do wrong, to hurt someone, to waste the gift. That's not gloom; it's taking life seriously.
The house of Hillel: better to be created.
A person is a chance for good that nothing else in the world can be. Then they counted, and the Talmud gives the verdict, which keeps both. It would have been better not to be created.
But now that we have been, let a person examine their deeds. That's the turn. The verdict doesn't settle whether life was a good idea in the abstract.
It hands the question back as work: you're here, so look at what you do. Hillel's three questions say the same in miniature. Be for yourself; nobody can do your part.
Don't be only for yourself. And don't wait. The odd part: the verdict leans toward 'better not,' and it still ends where Hillel's saying does.

how: Hillel's three questions, from Pirkei Avot, are studied in Jewish homes, schools and synagogues; the Talmud's debate between the houses of Hillel and Shammai is read in Eruvin 13b.

o: a saying that you should never plan ahead
a warning that the end of the world is near
Hillel's question: this moment is the time

games.q: who said what: tap the pairs.
p: now that we're here, examine our deeds

s: 'if not now, when?' is just a motivational slogan with no story behind it
in the Talmud, a long argument about whether life is worth it lands on the same place: now, examine your deeds.
the Talmud says the two houses argued for two and a half years
Eruvin 13b gives that span for the debate over whether humans should have been created.
Hillel taught to look after others and never yourself
his first question is 'if I am not for myself, who will be for me?' the second adds: not only for myself.

games.q: you're in the house of Hillel. to argue fairly, state the house of Shammai's best case for 'better not to be created.'
o: a life carries huge responsibility; every day we can do wrong or waste the gift.
life is mostly suffering, so nothing a person does really matters.
people are evil by nature, so making them was a mistake.
games.why: Shammai's side takes life so seriously it trembles at it. the verdict keeps that weight and turns it into work: examine your deeds.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Write the one thing you've been snoozing, something for yourself or for someone else, in a few plain words. Under it, write the smallest piece of it you could do today, and the hour you'll do it.

wordCard.voice: If not now: the end of Hillel's three questions, the one that refuses the snooze button. Im lo achshav in the Hebrew.

orig.note: Hebrew, Pirkei Avot 1:14: if not now, when?

carryVoice: Pocket this one: if not now, when, right where both houses ended up. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Pirkei Avot 1:14 (Hillel: if I am not for myself, who is for me? and if I am only for myself, what am I? and if not now, when?)

Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b (the houses of Shammai and Hillel debate two and a half years whether it would have been better for man not to be created; they conclude: better not, but now that he has been, let him examine his deeds)
